snippet.title: The Quaker Oats Family: The Name-Theft That Built America's Breakfast Empire
snippet.description:
In this in-depth, full-length documentary, we explore how a Presbyterian miller in Ravenna, Ohio named Henry Parsons Crowell sat down with an encyclopedia in 1877, read the entry on the Religious Society of Friends, and branded his oats with the name and image of a religious community he did not belong to and had no permission to use. He turned a grain Americans fed to horses into the first nationally trademarked food product in American history, won the late-nineteenth century Oatmeal War, built the company that became Quaker Oats, and left a 150-year-old name-theft sitting inside a $79.5 billion PepsiCo subsidiary.

----------------------------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

----------------------------------------

In 1755, Samuel Johnson defined oats in his dictionary as "a grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people." For more than a century after, Americans agreed with the English half of that definition. Oats were horse feed.

The first man to disagree was Ferdinand Schumacher, a German immigrant who arrived in Akron, Ohio in 1851 and began grinding oats for the German and Irish working-class immigrant population who already ate them. By the 1870s his German Mills American Oatmeal Factory was the largest oat mill in the country.

The man who took the category from him was Henry Parsons Crowell, born in 1855 in Cleveland to a wealthy Presbyterian family. Tuberculosis killed his father when Henry was eight. Henry was diagnosed with it himself in his early twenties and made a private vow to God: if his health was restored, he would devote his business earnings to evangelical Christian causes for the rest of his life.

In 1881 he bought a failing oat mill in Ravenna, Ohio. He needed a brand. He sat down with an encyclopedia, found the entry on the Religious Society of Friends, and chose the word "Quaker" for what he called its associations with honesty, purity, and plain dealing. He had no connection to the Religious Society of Friends. He never asked them.

In 1877 a Cleveland miller named William Heston had already trademarked the Quaker name and the image of a man in colonial dress, the first registered trademark for a breakfast cereal in the United States. By 1888 Heston, Schumacher, and Crowell had merged into the American Cereal Company. Crowell, the youngest of the three, was elected president.

He invented the modern branded food industry from that office. The cylindrical paperboard canister with the Quaker man on it was patented in 1915 and is still in use today. He pioneered the cereal box premium with miniature china dolls and metal whistles. He bought a full-page ad on the back cover of Ladies' Home Journal in 1891, then unheard of for a food product. He launched the first national radio advertising campaign for a breakfast cereal in 1924. He gave away free samples by the trainload, paying railway porters to hand them out at stations between Chicago and the West Coast.

In 1901 the company was reorganised as the Quaker Oats Company.

The Religious Society of Friends began objecting almost immediately. In 1915 the U.S. Congress declined to bar religious group names from trademark registration. The Friends World Committee for Consultation issued formal complaints in 1939, 1958, 1976, and 1999. None succeeded.

Crowell ran the company until 1922 and chaired its board until 1942. He gave away an estimated $70 million in his lifetime to the Moody Bible Institute and other evangelical causes, more than ninety percent of his fortune. He died in 1944.

The company continued. In the 1940s, MIT and Quaker Oats fed radioactive iron-laced oatmeal to mentally disabled children at the Fernald School in Massachusetts in an experiment that produced a 1998 settlement of approximately $1.85 million to the surviving subjects.

In 1994 Quaker Oats acquired Snapple for $1.7 billion. Three years later it sold the brand for $300 million. The CEO who made the deal, William Smithburg, resigned. The $1.4 billion writedown is still taught in business schools as a textbook overpayment.

In 2001 Quaker Oats was acquired by PepsiCo for $13.4 billion. The acquisition was driven by the Gatorade subsidiary the company had bought in 1983.

Larry the Quaker, the smiling man on the box, was modernised in 2012 and given a thinner face. He is still on every canister of Quaker Oats sold in America. He has never been a Quaker.

snippet.title: The Vanished Gilded Age Dynasty Richer Than Rockefeller's Own Sons: The Harkness Family
snippet.description:
In this in-depth, full-length documentary, we explore how Stephen V. Harkness, a harness-maker's stepson from Bellevue, Ohio, became the silent third partner in John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil in 1867, watched his stake grow into the second-largest individual fortune in the company, died on his yacht off the coast of Florida in 1888, and left behind a wife and son who, through three generations, gave away more than $250 million to Yale, Columbia, Harvard, and the Commonwealth Fund and then, by deliberate family policy, erased the Harkness name from public memory in the country they helped finance.

----------------------------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

----------------------------------------

Bellevue, Ohio in the 1850s was a railroad town between Sandusky and the interior, with a general store at its commercial center run by the extended Harkness clan. The store was where a teenage relation named Henry Morrison Flagler would learn the trade. Stephen Vanderburg Harkness, born in 1818, grew up there.

Stephen's first real fortune came from a Monroeville distillery he opened in 1855, sold to insiders shortly before the federal whiskey excise tax of 1862, and rolled into Cleveland real estate and finance.

In 1867 John D. Rockefeller needed capital to expand his Cleveland refining business and approached Flagler, who arranged an introduction to his step-relation Stephen Harkness. Harkness put in $100,000 on the condition that Flagler be brought into the firm as treasurer. The arrangement created Rockefeller, Andrews & Flagler. By the time Standard Oil incorporated in 1870, Harkness held the second-largest individual stake after Rockefeller himself.

He stayed silent. He held no operational role, attended no board meetings the public ever heard about, and was named by Rockefeller in 1910 as one of the founding holders of the majority of Standard Oil stock through its entire history.

He died on March 6, 1888, aboard his yacht The Twilight, approximately forty miles off Punta Gorda, Florida, at sixty-nine.

His widow Anna and his son Edward inherited a fortune estimated at $150 million in 1888 dollars, equivalent to roughly $5 billion today. Edward was twenty-eight. He had never worked in oil.

Edward Stephen Harkness spent the next forty-five years giving the money away. His foundation, the Commonwealth Fund, founded in 1918 by his mother and run by Edward after her death, gave more than $50 million to public-health research, child welfare, and medical education across the United States and the United Kingdom. He gave roughly $11 million to Columbia (the Harkness Pavilion at Columbia-Presbyterian, the Harkness Eye Institute), $13 million to Yale (the residential college system, Sterling Memorial Library), and substantial sums to Harvard (the river houses, Adams House) and to St. Paul's School.

He insisted on anonymity. The buildings carry the family name only because the universities pressed it on him over his objection. He gave no press interviews, attended no public banquets, and is the only American philanthropist of the early twentieth century with a fortune over $100 million who left no published portrait of himself except a single Yale-commissioned painting.

He died on January 29, 1940 in New York City at sixty-five, childless.

The fortune passed to his nephew William Hale Harkness, who died of a heart attack at fifty-four. William's widow Rebekah Harkness inherited approximately $720 million in 1954 (roughly $8 billion today) and spent the next forty years burning through every dollar of it as patron of the Harkness Ballet, the Harkness Atelier, the Harkness Foundation, and a string of estates in Watch Hill, New York City, and Switzerland. By her death in 1982 the family's principal fortune was effectively gone.

What remained, the Commonwealth Fund, the residential colleges at Yale, the Harkness Tower on Yale's Old Campus, the Sterling Library, the Adams House at Harvard, the Pavilion at Columbia, the medical school endowments, was the architecture of American higher education and American medical research in the twentieth century.

The mausoleum at Woodlawn Cemetery in the Bronx that James Gamble Rogers designed and Beatrix Farrand landscaped is the only building in America that carries the Harkness name in stone above the door. There are no streets named after them. There are no public statues. The harness-maker's stepson who held the second-largest stake in Standard Oil ensured that his descendants would be unfindable.

The Harkness family is the missing half of the Standard Oil story. They preferred it that way.

snippet.title: With $2 Billion in Oil, He Funded Joseph McCarthy, Eisenhower, and Half of Houston: Hugh Roy Cullen
snippet.description:
He was an 18-year-old cotton buyer with a fifth-grade education and three dollars a week of factory wages behind him when he decided he would never work for anyone but himself again. Fifty-five years later, Hugh Roy Cullen died as one of the richest men in America — a $2-to-$3 billion fortune in today's money pulled out of depleted salt domes that every major oil company had already written off, the head of the largest independent oil company in the American Southwest, and the most generous private donor any living American had ever produced. He gave away roughly 90 percent of what he made, building the University of Houston, the Texas Medical Center, and half the cultural institutions of modern Houston with the proceeds — and he used a significant portion of the rest to bankroll Joseph McCarthy, the Dixiecrats, and some of the most extreme political movements of the American mid-century.

———————————————————

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

———————————————————

Hugh Roy Cullen left school in the fifth grade to support his mother by sacking candy in a San Antonio factory for three dollars a week — and spent the rest of his childhood reading every book he could get his hands on, raised on stories of a grandfather who had been a hero of the Texas Revolution and the author of the law establishing Texas public education.

By 1901, he was an 18-year-old cotton buyer in Schulenburg, Texas, sharp at the work and engaged to a local rancher's 16-year-old daughter named Lillie Cranz, who would not be permitted to marry him until she turned 21.

He entered the oil business in 1918 as a complete amateur, partnering with Houston lumberman Big Jim Cheek to wildcat in fields the majors had already declared dry — and within two decades had become the largest independent oilman in the American Southwest by perfecting a single technique nobody else would touch: drilling deeper into salt domes that experts had pronounced exhausted.

The breakthrough came at Tom O'Connor Field in 1934, where Cullen's deeper drilling unlocked one of the largest oil discoveries in Texas history — a strike that vaulted him from regional operator to one of the four most powerful independent oilmen in the country, alongside H.L. Hunt, Clint Murchison, and Sid Richardson.

In 1947, Roy and Lillie Cullen established the Cullen Foundation with an endowment of working interests in oil and gas properties valued at approximately $160 million at the time — the single largest philanthropic gift ever made by a living American as of that year.

By the time he died in July 1957, the day after his 76th birthday, Cullen had given away approximately 90 percent of his fortune — a level of lifetime giving unmatched by any American of his era, including Rockefeller and Carnegie, both of whom did most of their philanthropy posthumously through trusts.

The University of Houston exists today essentially because Cullen decided in the 1930s that working men and women and their children needed a four-year university of their own — and personally underwrote the institution's transformation from a junior college into one of the largest research universities in Texas.

The Texas Medical Center, now one of the largest medical complexes in the world, received foundational gifts from Cullen that built multiple hospitals and research institutions, including the original campus that anchored the entire ecosystem.

Texas Southern University, St. John's School, the Houston Symphony, and the Houston Museum of Fine Arts all received transformative Cullen funding — making him, more than any other single individual, the architect of modern Houston's civic infrastructure.

The same fortune also bankrolled the Texas Regulars in 1944, the Dixiecrat campaign in 1948, and Senator Joseph McCarthy's 1952 re-election — of which Cullen was the single biggest contributor in the entire country.

He gave heavily to Dwight Eisenhower, helped shift American conservatism's financial center of gravity from the East Coast to the Southwest, and became, in the framing of historian Bryan Burrough, the principal financial fuel behind the rise of modern American conservatism across the second half of the twentieth century.

Since its founding, the Cullen Foundation has distributed more than $600 million in grants, primarily to Texas institutions — and in 2026, the Lillie and Roy Cullen Tower opens as part of Baylor College of Medicine's Health Sciences Park, funded in part through a $30 million commitment from the foundation and the three Cullen Trusts established in the 1970s.

snippet.title: The $4.8 Billion Sons Who Inherited An "Old Money" Empire And Walked Away: The Ziff Family
snippet.description:
Three sons inherited one of the great American publishing empires (the company that built PC Magazine, Car and Driver, and Stereo Review) and instead of fighting over it, expanding it, or running it into the ground, they did something almost no heir in American history has done. They sold the entire thing for $1.4 billion in 1994, took roughly $467 million each, and walked away. The publishing brand they abandoned went through bankruptcy and trades today at barely a billion. The fortune they built by leaving is now worth roughly $18.5 billion... twenty-first on the Forbes list of America's richest families.

-------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------

The story begins on November 1, 1927, when William B. Ziff Sr. and Bernard G. Davis founded Ziff-Davis Publishing in Chicago and launched Popular Aviation in the same month Charles Lindbergh's transatlantic flight ignited a national obsession with flight. Their formula — niche enthusiast magazines for readers with real purchasing authority — survived the Depression, World War II, and the television revolution.

When Ziff Sr. died December 20, 1953, his 23-year-old son William B. Ziff Jr. was studying philosophy in Heidelberg. He returned to take over a $5 million company and turned every title into the number one publication in its category by 1970 — Car and Driver, Flying, Skiing, Yachting, Stereo Review, Modern Bride.

In 1978, Ziff Jr. was diagnosed with terminal prostate cancer. In 1984, he put all 24 of his magazines on the market in a single 24-hour auction. CBS bought the consumer titles for $362.5 million. Rupert Murdoch's News Corp bought the trade publications for $350 million. The two largest magazine transactions ever recorded.

He held back one title: PC Magazine, acquired in 1982. He rebuilt the company around computers, launched ZDNet online in 1988, and turned PC Magazine into the ninth-largest magazine in America at $281 million in annual revenue. He outlived his cancer diagnosis by 28 years.

Around 1990, at the family compound "Gemini" in Manalapan, Florida, Bill gathered Dirk, Robert, and Daniel — none of them groomed as publishing successors. Dirk had a Columbia English degree and a Harvard MBA. Robert was a Harvard engineer and a Cornell Law valedictorian. Daniel was still at Columbia. Dirk proposed taking $500 million to invest more broadly. Bill agreed.

In 1992, the brothers seeded former Goldman banker Daniel Och with $100 million for a 10% stake in what became Och-Ziff Capital — a $40 billion hedge fund that IPO'd on the NYSE in 2007. After the 1994 sale closed, they founded Ziff Brothers Investments, a pure family office that never took outside capital. By 1997, it was managing roughly $4 billion across 300-400 employees.

In 2014, the brothers dissolved ZBI to invest independently. Dirk became the primary backer of the World Surf League and donated his collection of nearly 600 vintage guitars — including Leo Fender's first prototype Telecaster — to the Metropolitan Museum of Art for a permanent exhibition opening in 2027. Robert endowed professorships at Cornell and made headlines donating to Republican state senators who provided decisive votes for same-sex marriage in New York. Daniel invested in Bill Browder's Hermitage Capital Fund, placing him at the center of the Magnitsky Act.

The brothers' mother, Barbara Ingrid Beitz, was the daughter of Berthold and Else Beitz, recognized by Israel as "Righteous Among the Nations" for protecting Jewish people during the Holocaust.

The Manalapan estate they grew up on — 15.65 acres stretching from the Atlantic to Lake Worth — was listed in 2015 for $195 million. It sold for $94.17 million in 2021 to Netscape founder Jim Clark, who flipped it to Larry Ellison for $173 million, the largest residential sale in Florida history.

Bill Ziff Jr. died in 2006. The brand he built and his sons sold went through SoftBank, the dot-com crash, and bankruptcy. The fortune the sons built by walking away is now worth eighteen times what the company sold for.

snippet.title: Why South Florida Became the New Playground of the Rich
snippet.description:
#SouthFloridaWealth #BillionaireMigration #MiamiRichLife 

South Florida has quietly transformed into one of the most powerful wealth hubs on Earth. From the guarded islands of Miami to the golden shores of Palm Beach, this region has become the ultimate sanctuary for billionaires, financial dynasties, and America’s richest families. But what is truly driving this historic migration? Why are the world’s wealthiest leaving New York, Chicago, and California to build their future in Miami and West Palm Beach?

In this documentary, we break down the real forces behind South Florida’s meteoric rise. From Florida’s zero income tax and unbeatable estate laws, to the impenetrable privacy of islands like Fisher Island and Indian Creek, the appeal goes far beyond sunshine. This is a strategic move that protects wealth, legacy, and security on a scale unmatched anywhere else in America. 

We explore the growing roster of billionaires who now call this region home — hedge fund titans, tech founders, Wall Street giants, and old-money families who have reshaped Palm Beach for over a century. From luxury marinas filled with mega-yachts to the elite private schools, world-class dining, exclusive golf clubs, and the magnetic pull of “Wall Street South,” South Florida has engineered the perfect ecosystem for extreme wealth.

This is not a trend — it is a permanent shift in the geography of power.
Watch as we uncover why Miami and West Palm Beach have become the new playground of the rich, and why their influence is only going to grow from here.

At its peak, the fortune Marjorie Merriweather Post controlled was valued at approximately two hundred million dollars at the time of her death in nineteen seventy-three, equivalent to roughly one point five billion in modern currency, making her one of the wealthiest women in the history of the United States and the single most powerful figure in the American food industry for the better part of half a century.

snippet.title: The Tragic Family Behind Panda Express
snippet.description:
The man who made Panda Express possible never heard the name Panda Express. He was an illiterate peasant from the countryside outside Yangzhou, China — one of the great culinary capitals of the world — who never spent a day in school, taught himself to cook in kitchens across China, Taiwan, and Japan, and died of cancer in a California hospital in 1981 before anyone outside Pasadena knew his name. His son Andrew and daughter-in-law Peggy built a $7.5 billion empire from what he left behind. Forty years after his death, his photograph still greets diners who walk through the door of the original restaurant.

-------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------

Andrew Cherng was born in Yangzhou in April 1948 — a city whose Huaiyang cuisine UNESCO would later designate a Creative City of Gastronomy. His arrival coincided almost exactly with the final catastrophic phase of the Chinese Civil War. His father, Ming-Tsai, came from the rural peasantry outside the city, never went to school, and learned to cook through pure necessity.

The family fled to Taiwan, then to Yokohama in 1963, where Ming-Tsai worked as a head chef and arranged for teenage Andrew to enter a restaurant kitchen in Yokohama's Chinatown.

In 1966, Andrew immigrated alone to the United States to attend Baker University in Kansas, where he met Peggy Tsiang, born in Mawlamyine, Myanmar, to Chinese parents who later fled to Hong Kong. Peggy earned a doctorate in electrical engineering and worked at McDonnell Douglas coding battlefield simulators for the U.S. Air Force.

On June 8, 1973, the Cherngs opened Panda Inn at 3488 East Foothill Boulevard in Pasadena. The entire family worked for free, lived together in a two-bedroom apartment, and watched pedestrians walk away from the empty restaurant. Andrew's mother scattered salt on the sidewalk — a Chinese ritual to ward off bad spirits.

After eight years of slow growth, Panda Inn finally found its audience. Then in 1981, Ming-Tsai Cherng died of cancer at City of Hope National Medical Center in Duarte, California.

In October 1983, with grief and ambition moving together inseparably, Andrew and Peggy opened the first Panda Express inside the Glendale Galleria food court across from a Hot Dog on a Stick stand. Peggy left her position as software development manager at Comtal Corporation and brought engineering discipline to restaurant operations — building what the family claims was one of the first restaurant Point of Sale systems in America. In 1987, in-house chef Andy Kao created Orange Chicken in a Panda Express kitchen in Hawaii — direct conceptual lineage from Ming-Tsai's tangerine peel chicken.

The chain has grown past 2,400 locations globally — and the Cherngs have never franchised a single one.

In 2023, Andrew and Peggy donated $100 million to City of Hope — the single largest philanthropic contribution for cancer care in the hospital's history — establishing the Cherng Family Center for Integrative Oncology. "City of Hope was the hope," Andrew said. "They took care of him and took care of him very well." Their total philanthropy exceeds $400 million.

When the original Pasadena Panda Inn was renovated and reopened in 2024, a photograph of Ming-Tsai cooking over fire was placed at the entrance — the first thing diners see when they walk through the door.

He was an illiterate peasant from the countryside outside Yangzhou, China — one of the great culinary capitals of the world — who never spent a day in school, taught himself to cook in kitchens across China, Taiwan, and Japan, and died of cancer in a California hospital in 1981 before anyone outside Pasadena knew his name. His son Andrew and daughter-in-law Peggy built a $7.5 billion empire from what he left behind. Forty years after his death, his photograph still greets diners who walk through the door of the original restaurant.

-------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

-------------------

Andrew Cherng was born in Yangzhou in April 1948 — a city whose Huaiyang cuisine UNESCO would later designate a Creative City of Gastronomy. His arrival coincided almost exactly with the final catastrophic phase of the Chinese Civil War. His father, Ming-Tsai, came from the rural peasantry outside the city, never went to school, and learned to cook through pure necessity.

The family fled to Taiwan, then to Yokohama in 1963, where Ming-Tsai worked as a head chef and arranged for teenage Andrew to enter a restaurant kitchen in Yokohama's Chinatown.

In 1966, Andrew immigrated alone to the United States to attend Baker University in Kansas, where he met Peggy Tsiang, born in Mawlamyine, Myanmar, to Chinese parents who later fled to Hong Kong. Peggy earned a doctorate in electrical engineering and worked at McDonnell Douglas coding battlefield simulators for the U.S. Air Force.

On June 8, 1973, the Cherngs opened Panda Inn at 3488 East Foothill Boulevard in Pasadena. The entire family worked for free, lived together in a two-bedroom apartment, and watched pedestrians walk away from the empty restaurant. Andrew's mother scattered salt on the sidewalk — a Chinese ritual to ward off bad spirits.

After eight years of slow growth, Panda Inn finally found its audience. Then in 1981, Ming-Tsai Cherng died of cancer at City of Hope National Medical Center in Duarte, California.

In October 1983, with grief and ambition moving together inseparably, Andrew and Peggy opened the first Panda Express inside the Glendale Galleria food court across from a Hot Dog on a Stick stand. Peggy left her position as software development manager at Comtal Corporation and brought engineering discipline to restaurant operations — building what the family claims was one of the first restaurant Point of Sale systems in America. In 1987, in-house chef Andy Kao created Orange Chicken in a Panda Express kitchen in Hawaii — direct conceptual lineage from Ming-Tsai's tangerine peel chicken.

The chain has grown past 2,400 locations globally — and the Cherngs have never franchised a single one.

In 2023, Andrew and Peggy donated $100 million to City of Hope — the single largest philanthropic contribution for cancer care in the hospital's history — establishing the Cherng Family Center for Integrative Oncology. "City of Hope was the hope," Andrew said. "They took care of him and took care of him very well." Their total philanthropy exceeds $400 million.

When the original Pasadena Panda Inn was renovated and reopened in 2024, a photograph of Ming-Tsai cooking over fire was placed at the entrance — the first thing diners see when they walk through the door.

snippet.title: The Powerful Men Who Destroyed Hollywood's Greatest Women (Documentary)
snippet.description:
In this in-depth, full-length documentary compilation, we explore two of Old Hollywood's most haunting stories of women broken by the powerful men in their lives — Frances Ford Seymour, the wealthy heiress wife of screen legend Henry Fonda who took her own life inside an institution in 1950, and silent film queen Gloria Swanson, the highest-paid actress of the 1920s who became the secret mistress of Joseph P. Kennedy and was financially and emotionally ruined by him before he discarded her.

----------------------------------------

Gain FREE access to secret full-length documentaries on wealthy families "too scandalous for YouTube" by joining our newsletter: https://www.substack.com/@oldmoneyluxury

----------------------------------------

Frances Ford Seymour was a wealthy New York socialite and the second wife of one of America's most beloved leading men, Henry Fonda. She raised two future Hollywood icons, Jane and Peter Fonda, while privately enduring her husband's coldness, infidelity, and emotional cruelty.

In April 1950, she died at the Craig House sanitarium in Beacon, New York, ruled a suicide, leaving behind two young children, a fortune, and a famous husband who reportedly went onstage in a Broadway play the same night without telling his cast what had happened.

Gloria Swanson was the queen of silent film, the highest-paid actress in Hollywood in the 1920s, and a Paramount Pictures icon whose face defined the decade. Then she met Joseph P. Kennedy.

Kennedy installed himself as her business manager, mingled her finances with his own, bankrolled her vanity project "Queen Kelly" with director Erich von Stroheim, and conducted a years-long affair while remaining married to Rose Kennedy.

When the project collapsed and the affair ended, Swanson was left financially devastated, her career in decline, while Kennedy moved on to build the political dynasty that would put his son in the White House.

This is the story of two of the most powerful men of the twentieth century, and the brilliant, gifted women they used, broke, and walked away from.

snippet.title: The Political Rise of George H.W. Bush (1924-1989) | Full Documentary | American Experience PBS
snippet.description:
The man behind a political dynasty.

When George. H.W. Bush left the Oval Office in 1993, rejected after one tumultuous presidential term, his 30-year career in public service came to an abrupt and unexpected end. Despite soaring approval ratings following military victory in the Persian Gulf, his years as president after the war were marked by almost unrelieved decline. A sluggish economy and an earlier decision to raise taxes, despite an explicit campaign oath, led to his defeat. By the end of his term many observers dismissed him as an artifact of an irrelevant Cold War past. 

GEORGE H.W. BUSH reveals the 41st president as a pivotal player during a critical moment in U.S. and world history and in a powerful political dynasty, drawing upon unparalleled access to figures in George H.W. Bush’s private and public life, his personal letters, and interviews with his advisors and critics, including First Lady Barbara Bush, Condoleezza Rice, Colin Powell, Mikhail Gorbachev, and more.

PART ONE (1924-1989) follows George H.W. Bush from his childhood in Greenwich, CT, to his service in World War II, then on to the oil fields of West Texas where he became a leader of the Texas Republican party. The biography examines his role in the Watergate and Iran Contra Scandals, and his first months in the Oval Office during the fall of the Soviet Union.

snippet.title: The Gilded Age Heiresses Who Inherited Millions And Died With Nothing (Documentary)
snippet.description:
Barbara Hutton inherited the equivalent of $900 million at 21 and died with $3,500 in a Beverly Wilshire suite in 1979. Huguette Clark inherited a $200 million copper fortune in 1925, lived for 20 years in a hospital room she never medically needed, and let gifts of more than $40 million flow to the people allowed inside it. Gloria Vanderbilt, great great great granddaughter of Commodore Cornelius Vanderbilt, left her son Anderson Cooper roughly $1.5 million from a name that had once defined American capitalism. Three of the most envied heiresses of the 20th century. Two billion dollars between them at peak. And not one of them died with a fortune in her own hands.

In this video, we talk about what actually drained the largest heiress fortunes of the American century, including the seven Hutton marriages and the 53-day Rubirosa payout, the Beth Israel hospital gifts to nurse Hadassah Peri and Dr. Henry Singman, the two 1999 Clark wills written six weeks apart, the 1934 Vanderbilt custody trial that named Gloria "Poor Little Rich Girl" at ten, the 1993 lawsuit against attorney Thomas Andrews and psychiatrist Christ Zois, the Bellosguardo estate that stood empty for 60 years, the Cartier jade necklace that resold for $27 million, and the structural pattern of professional retainers, powers of attorney, and inheritance law that made every individual story end the same way.

snippet.title: Brooke Astor: The Last Grande Dame Who Died In Squalor While Her Son Stole Millions
snippet.description:
She was 105 years old, lying on a torn couch in a stained nightgown in her own Park Avenue duplex. The heat was off. The room smelled of dog urine. She had given away more than $195 million to the libraries, museums, parks and shelters of New York City across 38 years as president of the Vincent Astor Foundation. Her personal estate was worth $185 million. And the man who had cancelled her doctor visits, fired her best friend the butler, refused a $2,000 safety gate to stop her falling down her own stairs, and forged her signature on a codicil that redirected $60 million away from the New York Public Library was her only son.

In this video, we talk about the rise and ruin of Brooke Astor including her violent first marriage at 17 to Dryden Kuser, the broken jaw before her son was born, the great love marriage to Charles Marshall, the calculated 1953 marriage to Vincent Astor that gave her control of $125 million, the 38-year reign at the Vincent Astor Foundation and the $195 million she gave back to New York, Anthony Marshall's decorated career as a Marine at Iwo Jima and US Ambassador, his 1992 marriage to Charlene Gilbert that her mother-in-law openly despised, the 2002 will that left Charlene only a necklace and two used fur coats, the three codicils of 2003 and 2004, the $920,000 yacht and the refused $2,000 safety gate, the 2006 petition by grandson Philip Marshall supported by Annette de la Renta, David Rockefeller and Henry Kissinger, the 2009 conviction of Anthony Marshall on 14 counts and Francis Morrissey on 5, the forged signature on the third codicil, and the 2012 settlement that returned $100 million to the charities.
